questions: Describe a person who has influenced you

sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about my high school literature teacher, Mrs Hoa, who has had a lasting influence on me. I first met her when I was fifteen, and she taught me for three years. What made her special was the way she turned every lesson into a story. Instead of just asking us to memorise facts, she encouraged us to discuss books freely and to explain what we really thought. I was quite shy back then, but she kept giving me small chances to speak in front of the class. Little by little, I gained the confidence to share my ideas. One thing she said has stayed with me ever since: that a good answer is not the correct one, but the honest one. I think that changed how I approach problems, both at work and in everyday life. I no longer worry so much about being wrong, and I'm much more willing to try. She also introduced me to reading for pleasure, which is now one of my favourite habits. Although we lost touch after I graduated, I still think of her whenever I finish a good book. To be honest, I believe she is the main reason I became a more curious and open-minded person. She showed me that a teacher can do far more than deliver information; they can change the way a young person sees themselves. If I ever get the chance, I would love to thank her in person and tell her how much she meant to me.

questions: Describe a memorable trip you have taken
cueCard: and explain why this trip was memorable for you
sampleAnswer: I'd like to describe a trip to Ha Giang that I took with two of my cousins about two years ago. We rented motorbikes in Hanoi and spent four days riding along winding mountain roads in the far north of Vietnam. The scenery was absolutely breathtaking. In the mornings, the valleys were covered in mist, and by lunchtime the sun lit up the rice terraces and the rocky peaks. We stopped in small villages to eat noodles and drink local tea, and we took far too many photos. Admittedly, the trip was tiring, and on the second day we got lost in heavy rain. Luckily, a local family invited us into their home, gave us hot tea and even let us stay the night. That unexpected kindness turned out to be the highlight of the whole journey. We sat around the fire, chatted with the family using a mix of gestures and a few words, and ate a simple but delicious meal. I think this trip was memorable not only because of the beautiful landscape, but also because of the people we met. It taught me that the best travel experiences are often the ones you don't plan. Since then, I've been keen to travel more slowly and talk to locals. I'm hoping to go back next autumn, when the rice terraces turn golden, and maybe bring my parents along this time.

questions: Describe a book you have read and enjoyed

sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about a novel called The Alchemist, written by Paulo Coelho. It's a fairly short book, but it left a deep impression on me. The story follows a young Spanish shepherd named Santiago, who has a recurring dream about hidden treasure near the Egyptian pyramids. He decides to leave his familiar life behind and travel across the desert to find it. Along the way, he meets many interesting people, including an old king, a merchant and a wise alchemist, who each teach him something about life. I decided to read it after a close friend recommended it to me when I was feeling uncertain about my career. She said it had helped her to stay motivated, so I thought it was worth a try. I finished it in just three evenings because I simply couldn't put it down. What I enjoyed most was the simple, almost poetic language and the central message that we should follow our dreams, even when the path is difficult. Of course, some critics find the story a bit predictable, and I can understand that. Nevertheless, it came at the right moment in my life and gave me the courage to change jobs. I've since reread it twice, and each time I notice something new. I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who feels stuck and needs a little inspiration.

In the summer, you can even see families flying kites or couples taking wedding photos. The reason it helps me relax is that it feels very different from the noisy streets in the city centre. The air is cooler, the view is open and wide, and the sound of the water is calming. After a stressful day at work, even half an hour there makes me feel much lighter. I also like the fact that it's free and open to everyone, so you see all kinds of people enjoying themselves. questions: Describe a time when you helped someone
cueCard: and explain how you felt about it
sampleAnswer: I'd like to tell you about a time I helped an elderly neighbour, Mr Binh, who lives on the floor below me. A few months ago, he fell on the stairs and hurt his leg, so he couldn't go out to buy groceries or collect his medicine. His children live in another city, and he didn't want to bother them. I only found out because I heard him calling for help one evening. I called an ambulance, stayed with him until it came, and then went with him to the hospital. Fortunately, it wasn't a serious injury, but the doctor told him to rest for a few weeks. During that time, I did his shopping, picked up his medicine and sometimes brought him a hot meal after work. I also taught him how to use a video calling app so he could talk to his grandchildren, which he really enjoyed. At first, he kept apologising and saying he was a burden, but I assured him that it was no trouble at all. In fact, I felt very happy to be useful. It made me realise how isolated some older people can feel in big cities, even when they live in a building full of neighbours. Since then, we've become good friends, and he often invites me for tea and tells me stories about his youth. Helping him taught me that small acts of kindness can make a big difference, and I'm determined to look out for my neighbours more often.

questions: Describe a festival or celebration that is important in your country
cueCard: and explain why it is important to people in your country
sampleAnswer: The festival I'd like to describe is the Mid-Autumn Festival, which takes place in September or October, on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month. It's often called the Children's Festival, because it's a special time for kids. In the weeks before, the streets fill up with colourful lanterns, masks and stalls selling mooncakes. On the night itself, families gather to share a meal, eat mooncakes and enjoy fruit like pomelos and persimmons. Children carry paper lanterns and join lion dances in the neighbourhood, while adults sit outside and admire the full moon. I remember as a child waiting all day for the evening, because my father always helped me make a lantern in the shape of a star. What I like most about the festival is the warm, relaxed mood. It's not as hectic as the Lunar New Year, but it brings people together just the same. In my view, it's important because it reminds us to value family and to care about children. It also keeps old traditions alive, such as lantern making and lion dancing, which might otherwise be forgotten as life becomes more modern. Nowadays, many people give mooncakes to colleagues and friends as gifts, and some worry the festival is becoming too commercial. Still, whenever I look up at the bright moon with my family, I feel that the spirit of the festival is very much alive.

Ideally, I'd take a course in journalism or creative writing, and learn at least one more foreign language. As for the working conditions, I imagine they'd be quite unpredictable. I also like the thought that my writing could inspire others to travel responsibly and respect local communities. I realise it's a competitive field, but I'm willing to work hard. questions: What are the positive and negative effects of tourism on a local area?

sampleAnswer: Tourism brings clear benefits, such as jobs, investment and a boost to local businesses. In many regions it's the main source of income. However, there are drawbacks as well. In some cases, local culture is turned into a product for visitors, which can make it feel less authentic. I think the key is balance. If tourism is managed carefully, for example by limiting visitor numbers and encouraging small, locally owned businesses, communities can enjoy the benefits without losing what makes their home special.

sampleAnswer: Technology has transformed communication in several ways. questions: How has people's diet changed in your country over the past few decades?
Do you think traditional food will disappear in the future?
Why do some people prefer fast food even though they know it's unhealthy?
What role does food play in bringing people together?
sampleAnswer: Diets have changed dramatically over the past few decades. Rising incomes and urbanisation mean people now eat far more meat, sugar and processed food than their grandparents did, whereas traditional diets relied heavily on rice, vegetables and fish. Convenience has played a major part in this shift, since long working hours leave little time for cooking. While I don't think traditional cuisine will vanish altogether, there is a genuine risk that younger generations lose the skills and patience needed to prepare it. That would be a shame, as food is not merely nutrition but also a carrier of history and identity.

questions: Why do some people volunteer while others don't?
Is it the government's responsibility to help people in need, or individuals'?
Do you think people are less willing to help strangers than in the past?
How can communities encourage a stronger sense of belonging?
sampleAnswer: People volunteer for a variety of reasons, but I think a sense of purpose is often central. Those who give their time tend to feel they are contributing to something larger than themselves, which can be deeply satisfying. Others may be motivated by practical benefits, such as gaining experience for a career. Conversely, those who don't volunteer often cite lack of time rather than lack of care, particularly in societies where working hours are long. In my opinion, employers and schools could do more to remove this barrier, for instance by offering paid volunteering days. That would encourage participation and, ultimately, strengthen communities.
